description.fun: A tiny bird with a huge attitude, Rookidee will pick a fight with anything, however big, and even a defeat leaves it a little stronger. Females are fussier than males: dirty a female Rookidee's wings and it will peck you relentlessly. Hitoshi Ariga designed the whole line, from this tit-like chick to the armoured Corviknight.
description.guide: A small Flying-type bird of Galar, modelled on tits such as the blue tit. Rookidee bravely challenges any opponent and grows a little stronger from every battle, even a loss. It evolves into Corvisquire and then Corviknight.
description.tagline: Picks fights it can't win and grows stronger anyway

description.fun: A brainy crow that uses tools in battle, flinging rocks and tying up foes with vines or rope. Its brain is large for a bird Pokémon's, and hard battles have taught it to size up an opponent before it engages. Its tool use may nod to the New Caledonian crow, famous for the same trick.
description.guide: The middle stage of Rookidee's line, a crow-like Pokémon based on corvids found in Britain such as the jackdaw. Corvisquire is intelligent enough to use tools in battle and judges an opponent's strength before fighting.
description.tagline: A tool-using crow that sizes you up before it fights

description.fun: The strongest bird in Galar's skies, armoured in steel feathers like a black knight, also runs the region's Flying Taxi service. In Paldea it can't do the job: Tinkaton pelt it with rocks mid-flight, so taxis there use Squawkabilly instead. Its look may draw on the ravens kept at the Tower of London.
description.guide: The final evolution of Rookidee, a large steel-armoured raven said to be the strongest bird Pokémon in Galar. Corviknight carries passengers for the region's Flying Taxi service. It has a Gigantamax form.
description.tagline: Galar's armoured raven, and its taxi service

description.fun: Its wings whip up winds stronger than a hurricane, and the eight 'blade bird' feathers on its back can launch off and attack foes on their own.
